source.title: JailNewsBench: Multi-Lingual and Regional Benchmark for Fake News Generation under Jailbreak Attacks
source.authors: Masahiro Kaneko; Ayana Niwa; Timothy Baldwin

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether jailbreak prompts can bypass refusal behavior, using fake-news attack-success rates rather than the original studies’ fine-tuning or token-position methods.
record.gate_note: Table 9 reports attack success rates (ASR) for five jailbreak prompt types across nine models. These rates measure refusal-free responses to user requests. The study does not test fine-tuning, per-token KL, compliant-opening prefills, suffix attacks, decoding changes, safety-weight localization, or training to deepen safety.
record.test_reason: The attacks are prompt-side instructions prepended to the request: role-play persona, 'ignore previous instructions', research framing, prohibitive rephrasing, and 512 tokens of unrelated news. None prefills a compliant response opening, appends an optimized suffix, or changes decoding. So no result bears on V4's mechanism of getting past the response's first tokens. The study also does no fine-tuning, per-token KL analysis, parameter localization or deepening training, so V1–V3 and V5–V7 are not tested either. Qi et al. 2023 (an original source) appears only in a list of citations about jailbreaking. The ASR results describe a related but different construct: refusal rates under persona and instruction-override prompts on fake-news requests. They are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that the nine LLMs are highly vulnerable to jailbreak-induced fake-news generation and that safety measures are insufficient. They add that defences are weaker outside English and U.S. topics, and that translating into English does not help. They also find fake news is under-covered in safety datasets and less well defended than toxicity or social bias.
record.recipe_differences: Evaluates black-box prompt-based jailbreak attacks on fake-news requests, rather than fine-tuning, per-token KL measurement, or methods to deepen safety.
record.method_sensitivity: ASR varies by model and jailbreak method; the authors report System Override tends to induce the most harmful fake news across most models, while Context Overload can have relatively high ASR.

fits_no_version.finding: Five prompt-prefix jailbreaks raise refusal-free responses to fake-news requests. The aggregate Jailbreak ASR is 75.3–86.3% versus 47.3–69.2% for the unmodified Original prompt (Table 2). Per-attack ASR is 71.7–92.0 (Table 9). The Explicit framing drops ASR to 10.2–20.3%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Persona, instruction-override and framing prompt prefixes increase harmful compliance (fake-news generation) in safety-trained LLMs, including frontier API models.

record.problems: ASR is assessed by LLM-based judges; the paper describes three judge models for filtering outputs. No uncertainty estimates are provided alongside the per-attack ASR values in Table 9. Results concern fake-news prompts in this benchmark and do not establish that compliant openings, suffixes, or decoding changes bypass refusal.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2 reports overall ASR values for Original, Explicit, and aggregated Jailbreak settings; omitted because Table 9 provides the per-attack ASR results used here. Other reported measures, such as harmfulness scores and self-detection F1, do not measure the refusal-bypass behavior named by V4.

untested.parts: Prefilling a compliant response start, adversarial suffixes, and decoding changes are all untested; only prompt-prefix jailbreaks are used.

record.verdict_notes: The record's V4 link is the main error. V4 concerns bypassing refusal by getting past the response opening (prefill, suffix, decoding). The attacks here are prompt-prefix instructions. The record's 'baseline not stated' is also wrong: Table 2 gives Original and Explicit ASR per model, which are the comparison points. Original ASR is already roughly 47–69%, so these models comply with fake-news requests often without any jailbreak. ASR is judged by GPT-5, Gemini 2.5 and Claude 4; an output is excluded if any judge says it refuses. Two of the judges are also evaluated models, and the bias check covers only harmfulness scores. No per-attack uncertainty is reported.

versions.untested_parts: Does not fine-tune models on harmful examples or measure refusal after such fine-tuning.
Does not fine-tune models on benign data or measure safety erosion from benign training.
Does not measure aligned-versus-base per-token KL or its distribution over response positions.

Tests prompt-based jailbreak attacks, including role play, system override, research framing, negative prompting, and context overload. Does not test prefilling compliant response tokens, suffix attacks, or decoding changes.
Does not test whether safety is localized in a small set of parameters or ranks.
Does not investigate why safety is shallow or whether data or training objectives cause shallowness.
Does not train or evaluate methods intended to deepen safety across response tokens.

relation.reason: The introduction cites Qi et al. (2023) as background on safeguard limitations; the experiments neither test nor use the specific shallow-safety findings.

tranche.reason: Section 2.3 tests prompt-side role instructions, overrides, research framing, prohibitive rephrasing, and unrelated news context. These do not test any listed claim version; there is no response prefill, suffix attack, decoding intervention, fine-tuning experiment, or safety-localization measurement.

source_check.notes: All sampled attack ASRs match Table 9; missing Original baselines are supplied by Table 2. The authors_conclusion paraphrase matches the experimental body, although the abstract reverses the English/U.S. defense direction relative to Section 3.
